cards.title: Compact metric spaces without polynomially admissible representations
cards.formal: Does there exist a nonempty compact metric space (X,d) that has no polynomially admissible representation over Cantor space, in the quantitative sense of the cited Lim–Ziegler theory? The central existence question is recovered, but the treatment of continuous competitors without a global modulus still needs to be reconciled with the source definition.
cards.why: Asks whether compactness alone guarantees a representation with controlled information overhead. A counterexample would identify a limitation of encoding continuous data that persists even after changing the representation, rather than merely exposing a poor choice of coordinates.
cards.status_note: Source, cited preprint and the 2025 journal abstract checked through 11 September 2026. No matching general counterexample or all-compact-spaces theorem was located. The representation-domain convention remains unresolved in this formulation review.

sentences: A representation supplies infinite names for points in a compact metric space.
Polynomial admissibility compares the information required by those names with the space’s covering entropy and with competing representations.
The source asks whether any compact metric space admits no such representation at all.
The polynomial comparison concerns moduli of continuity rather than polynomial running time.
The intended convention for continuous competitors without a global modulus must still be reconciled with the published definition.

cards.definitions: A metric space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. Cantor space C={0,1}^ℕ has metric D(p,q)=2^(−min{k:pₖ≠qₖ}) for p≠q and D(p,p)=0, with coordinates indexed from zero. A representation of X is a partial surjection ξ:Dξ⊆C→X; points may have multiple names. Let K_X(n) be the smallest number of closed radius-2^(−n) balls centered in X that cover X, and set η_X(n)=⌈log₂K_X(n)⌉. A modulus of a map h between metric spaces is a nondecreasing μ:ℕ→ℕ such that inputs at distance at most 2^(−μ(n)) have outputs at distance at most 2^(−n). Its minimal modulus is the pointwise least such function, when one exists. For representations ξ and ξ′ with minimal moduli μ and μ′, a polynomial reduction in the cited v5 is a map G:Dξ′→Dξ satisfying ξ′=ξ∘G and having a modulus ν with ν(μ(n))≤μ′(p(n)) for some nondecreasing polynomial p with nonnegative integer coefficients. The polynomial may depend on the two representations and the reduction. Definition 14(b) further requires μ(n)≤η_X(q(n)) for some such polynomial q and requires every continuous partial surjection ξ′ from C onto X to reduce to ξ. No computability or polynomial running-time requirement on G is imposed by this topological definition. The finite-modulus clause and the quantification over all continuous partial surjections need reconciliation: continuous maps on noncompact partial domains need not be uniformly continuous. Restricting competitors to compact domains, restricting them to uniformly continuous maps, or extending the modulus notion are different formal choices that are not silently made here.
cards.answer_criterion: With the intended quantitative-admissibility definition fixed, exhibit a nonempty compact metric space and prove that every representation of it fails admissibility, or prove that every such space has an admissible representation. Showing that one particular encoding is inefficient does not rule out all encodings. The optional broader characterization in the seminar is not required by this central existence target.

context_blocks.title: Names reveal a point at increasing precision
context_blocks.text: An infinite bit stream can describe a real number or a function. The question is whether some naming system exposes the required accuracy with close to the information that the space itself demands. Multiple names for one point are allowed and can avoid discontinuities caused by rigid encodings.

context_blocks.title: Entropy measures the amount of information
context_blocks.text: If X needs K balls at a prescribed precision, selecting a ball requires about log₂K bits. For [0,1], this grows linearly with the precision index; for more complicated compact spaces it can grow much faster. The admissibility comparison therefore allows a polynomial change in the precision argument of entropy, rather than requiring polynomial entropy.

context_blocks.title: Quantitative continuity is not a running-time bound
context_blocks.text: A modulus bounds how many input bits determine a desired number of output bits. It says nothing by itself about how much computation is needed to obtain those output bits. The word polynomial in this question concerns relative moduli; replacing it with a polynomial-time translation would change the problem.

context_blocks.title: Existing positive results and the remaining scope
context_blocks.text: The cited preprint supplies sufficient conditions for quantitative representations, and the 2025 journal abstract reports a large class of compact metric spaces with such representations over compact ultrametric spaces. This is not an abstract-level claim that every compact metric space has one over the fixed Cantor ground space. The precise domain convention remains material.

statement_review.remaining_issue: The cited v5 Definition 14(a) defines polynomial reduction for maps with finite global moduli, whereas 14(b)(ii) quantifies over every continuous partial surjection from Cantor space. A partial domain need not be compact and continuity alone does not imply a finite global modulus. The intended restriction or extension for such competitors must be reconciled with the journal definition before certifying the proposition. The fixed-Cantor question must also be distinguished from existence over more general compact ultrametric ground spaces. The 2025 journal abstract was checked, but its full definition was not available in this review.

cards.title: Explicit input pairs resistant to partial monotone separation
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist families of nonempty disjoint sets Aₙ,Bₙ⊆{0,1}ⁿ, each with a uniform NP membership predicate, and an integer-valued function r(n)≥0 with r(n)/log₂log₂n→∞, such that the families are compatible with monotone separation and every monotone circuit separating a 2^(−r(n)) fraction of Aₙ from a 2^(−r(n)) fraction of Bₙ, in either direction, has size n^ω(1)?
cards.why: Seeks explicit input distributions for which the monotone lower-bound obstruction survives both severe restriction of the tested inputs and reversal of labels. This robustness is tied to understanding how a limited use of negation changes circuit power, beyond ordinary monotone complexity.

sentences: The problem asks for explicit disjoint families of Boolean inputs that are hard to distinguish using monotone circuits.
A circuit may separate only a small fraction of each family and may reverse the output labels.
Both membership predicates must have uniform polynomially checkable witnesses under the book’s explicitness convention.

references.title: Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers (author's early draft)

cards.definitions: All claims are for integers n≥4, with finitely many initial lengths irrelevant. Explicitness is interpreted for both membership predicates using the book’s Section 1.5.1: there are fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifiers V_A,V_B and fixed polynomial witness bounds p_A,p_B such that x∈Aₙ iff some y∈{0,1}^≤p_A(n) satisfies V_A(x,y)=1, and analogously for Bₙ. This does not require listing exponentially many members. Compatibility with a monotone separator means that no b∈Bₙ and a∈Aₙ have b≤a coordinatewise; equivalently, some monotone Boolean function is zero on Aₙ and one on Bₙ. A monotone circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input variables x₁,…,xₙ, constants 0 and 1, and fan-in-two AND and OR gates, no negations, unrestricted fan-out and one output. Size is its number of AND/OR gates. Write θₙ=2^(−r(n)). A circuit C partially separates the pair if either Pr_{a uniform in Aₙ}[C(a)=0]≥θₙ and Pr_{b uniform in Bₙ}[C(b)=1]≥θₙ, or Pr_{a uniform in Aₙ}[C(a)=1]≥θₙ and Pr_{b uniform in Bₙ}[C(b)=0]≥θₙ. The two probabilities use their separate finite uniform distributions; no condition is imposed on the remaining inputs. Thus the circuit may choose which subsets it separates, and integer subset sizes are rounded up by the displayed fraction inequalities. The required superpolynomial bound means: for every constant k>0 there is n_k such that for all n≥n_k, every partially separating monotone circuit has more than n^k gates. There is no uniformity restriction on these circuits. The growth condition on r means that for every constant c>0, eventually r(n)>c log₂log₂n. No independent time bound is required for evaluating the displayed function r.
cards.answer_criterion: Give explicit membership verifiers for both input families, a function r with the required growth, and a proof of monotone compatibility and the superpolynomial lower bound for every permitted partial separator in both directions; or prove that no such families and r exist. Hardness only for separating all of A from all of B in one direction does not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Hard on two small portions, in either direction
context_blocks.text: The usual monotone separation task rejects every negative input and accepts every positive input. Here a circuit is allowed to handle only small subsets of each side, and may reverse the output labels. As r grows, the required fractions shrink, so the hardness claim becomes stronger.

context_blocks.title: Why reversing the labels changes the problem
context_blocks.text: Suppose all inputs in A have Hamming weight at least ten and all inputs in B have weight at most nine. The monotone threshold circuit that accepts weights at least ten separates the entire pair in the reverse direction. Regardless of the difficulty of the forward direction, such a pair cannot meet the required two-direction hardness.

context_blocks.title: The small fractions are measured separately
context_blocks.text: For example, r=3 requires correct separation on at least one eighth of A and one eighth of B. A circuit may behave arbitrarily on the rest. This is not a single average-error requirement on the union, where a larger side could conceal failure on the smaller side.

context_blocks.title: The connection to negations
context_blocks.text: The book relates this robust pair property to lower bounds for circuits containing a limited number of NOT gates. It reports an r of order log log n from Amano and Maruoka’s work and identifies logarithmic r as sufficient for a breakthrough on unrestricted circuit size. Those are dated source statements; the requested improvement is any r growing faster than log log n.

context_blocks.title: A related later measure is different
context_blocks.text: The later negation-width paper controls how many distinct negated variables occur in syntactically produced terms. Its lower bounds do not by themselves exhibit a pair satisfying the two separate fraction conditions here. A bound involving negation width cannot be substituted for the requested r-hard pair.

cards.title: Complexity assumptions implying time-space lower bounds for composition
cards.formal: Can strong time-space lower bounds for composing low-space algorithms, such as the hypothesis of Pyne–Tell’s Theorem 3.8, be derived from independently specified complexity assumptions? The source’s admissible assumptions and its selected lower-bound variant remain unspecified.
cards.why: Would connect the cost of reusing small-memory computations to established complexity assumptions and to derandomization. Such a connection would explain whether a broad composition barrier follows from familiar hardness principles rather than standing as an isolated new assumption.

sentences: Two individually memory-efficient algorithms can have a composition with a larger time-space cost.

cards.definitions: A low-space algorithm is a uniform deterministic computation using O(log n) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output, where n is the original input length. If A₁ outputs a binary string accepted as input by A₂, their composition maps x to A₂(A₁(x)). An algorithm for the composition may compute this function by any means; it need not run the two supplied programs in sequence. A time-space product is t(n)s(n), where t and s bound running time and work space on length-n inputs in the selected machine model. Correctness on an ε fraction means Pr_{x uniform in {0,1}ⁿ}[B(x)=A₂(A₁(x))]≥ε, with exact equality of the complete output strings. The motivating hypothesis has quantifier pattern ∃δ>0 ∀polynomial T ∀constant ε>0 ∃low-space A₁,A₂ with individual time O(T(n)), such that every deterministic algorithm computing their composition on an ε fraction requires a product of order at least T(n)^(1+δ). Both stages’ time bounds are measured as functions of the original n; the first may output up to O(T(n)) bits. The survey states this informally using a single f, while the underlying paper uses two algorithms and explains length conventions. The precise eventual/input-length and machine-model version belongs to the selected final hypothesis. BPL consists of languages decided with O(log n) space, polynomial time and error at most 1/3; L uses deterministic O(log n) space. The displayed consequence BPL⊆⋂_{ε>0}avg_εL means that for each BPL language and each fixed ε>0, a deterministic logspace algorithm agrees with it on at least a 1−ε fraction of uniformly distributed inputs at all sufficiently large lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: For a fixed independently stated and admissible complexity hypothesis H and a fixed composition lower-bound statement C, prove the implication H⇒C or refute that precise implication. A weaker statement for only one small polynomial time bound does not establish a claim quantified over every polynomial T. The currently unspecified family of acceptable assumptions prevents this card from being one completed implication.

context_blocks.title: Computing a composition can cost more than either stage
context_blocks.text: Two programs can each use very little working memory while passing a long intermediate string between them. Storing that string consumes space; avoiding its storage can increase time. The question concerns lower bounds on the function itself, including algorithms that do not materialize the intermediate string.

context_blocks.title: The measure is a product of two resources
context_blocks.text: A bound t(n)s(n)≥n^1.33 allows different compromises. For example, under a linear-time restriction it forces polynomial space, while under a logarithmic-space restriction it forces a superlinear time bound. It does not state that every implementation must use polynomial space regardless of time.

context_blocks.title: A restricted unconditional barrier is known
context_blocks.text: The revised composition paper exhibits two linear-time logspace transformations whose composition has an n^1.33 time-space lower bound, even when correctness is required on only a constant fraction of inputs. This establishes a barrier for that time range, but not the hypothesis for every polynomial T.

context_blocks.title: Why the stronger hypothesis matters
context_blocks.text: The paper shows that suitable superlinear time-space tradeoffs for all polynomial time bounds would yield deterministic logspace simulations of BPL that are correct on almost all uniformly distributed inputs. The survey’s question asks for independent foundations for those tradeoffs; it does not already establish the tradeoffs or full BPL=L.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.
